## A Detailed History of Mount Gretna, Pennsylvania

Mount Gretna, Pennsylvania, developed from a resource-rich woodland area into a unique center for summer recreation, religious fellowship, and cultural arts. Its history is defined by its dual identity as a destination for Chautauqua education and a location for Evangelical United Brethren camp meetings, evolving from an early amusement park to a modern artistic community.

### Unique Founding and Subdivisions
Mount Gretna originated in a forest of chestnut trees, which historically provided charcoal for the **Cornwall Furnace**, a site that once forged cannons for George Washington’s army [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

The site was first noted in **1883** as a pleasant place for a summer day along the extinct Cornwall and Lebanon Railroad [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

The town developed through two closely related, yet distinct, founding movements in **1892**:

1.  **The Pennsylvania Chautauqua:** Founded by members of the Evangelical United Brethren, this movement modeled itself after the original Chautauqua Institution (1874, New York). They built a vaulted conical-roofed outdoor auditorium (the Playhouse) and a Hall of Philosophy for lectures, concerts, and religious services, subsequently constructing summer cottages [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].
2.  **The Camp Meeting:** The United Brethren also established a camp meeting across Pinch Road, hiring the same builder to construct a Tabernacle for religious services and Bible meetings. Worshipers built 100 cottages around tent plots [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

### Religious and Cultural History
The initial success of Mount Gretna was rooted in both educational and religious gatherings. The **Chautauqua** provided structured learning alongside leisure, while the **Camp Meeting** provided a dedicated space for Bible conferences and worship [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

**Cultural History:** The town experienced a cultural peak in the early 20th century, hosting concerts, lectures, and trade shows [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/]. Following a period of decline, a modern cultural revival began around **1976** with the **First Annual Outdoor Art Show**, initiated by local artists (Bruce Johnson, Reed Dixon, and John Wenzler). This fostered the growth of **Gretna Theatre** and **Music at Gretna**, establishing the community as a recognized regional center for arts and culture [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

### Military History
Military activity began relatively early in the town's development; the **Pennsylvania National Guard** started a 50-year annual encampment at Mt. Gretna in **1885** [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/]. Mount Gretna served as the state's first dedicated permanent training area. Furthermore, Mount Gretna is noted as a predecessor site to **Fort Indiantown Gap** [Source: https://www.ftig.ng.mil/About-Us/News/Article/4232222/mount-gretna-fort-indiantown-gaps-predecessor/].

### Summer Recreation Site Status and Attractions
Mount Gretna initially thrived as an early amusement park destination. Attractions included a stone fountain, an elaborate carousel, a primitive roller coaster called a “switch-back,” and a dancing pavilion [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

In **1885**, Conewago Creek was dammed to form **Lake Conewago**, which became a central feature for swimming and canoeing [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/]. The narrow gauge railroad (1889) allowed visitors to reach the top of Governor Dick Hill for expansive views [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

The peak recreational period lasted for about two decades. However, the rise of the **automobile** led to decline after the 1920s, compounded by the Depression and the departure of the National Guard in 1933. The amusement park closed, and the narrow gauge was abandoned [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

### Businesses Since Founding
Several businesses have existed in Mount Gretna since its founding, though many have closed and reopened:

*   **Early Businesses:** The initial attractions included park facilities, and lodging/retail included the **Chautauqua Inn**, **The Conewago Hotel** (1909, known for early modern amenities like private baths and telephones), **Kaufman’s Store and Hotel**, and **The Jigger Shop Ice cream parlor** [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].
*   **Enduring/Later Businesses:** The **Jigger Shop** continued to operate later in the century. The **Chautauqua Inn** survived the closures of other large hotels, though it was eventually demolished in **1970** due to modern fire codes and liability concerns [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/]. The **Timber Restaurant** was built in the **1960s** [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/]. Today, the arts and cultural organizations (Gretna Theatre, Music at Gretna) and local businesses supporting the Art Show provide economic support [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

**Note on Continuity:** While many early establishments have closed (e.g., the Conewago Hotel, Kaufman Hotel), the *tradition* of gathering—in the Playhouse, at the Campmeeting, on the porches, and through the Jigger Shop—has been a constant thread throughout the town's history [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

## A Detailed History of Mount Gretna, Pennsylvania

Mount Gretna, Pennsylvania, developed from a resource-rich woodland area into a unique center for summer recreation, religious fellowship, and cultural arts. Its history is defined by its dual identity as a destination for Chautauqua education and a location for Evangelical United Brethren camp meetings, evolving from an early amusement park to a modern artistic community.

### Unique Founding and Subdivisions
Mount Gretna originated in a forest of chestnut trees, which historically provided charcoal for the **Cornwall Furnace**, a site that once forged cannons for George Washington’s army [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

The site was first noted in **1883** as a pleasant place for a summer day along the extinct Cornwall and Lebanon Railroad [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

The town developed through two closely related, yet distinct, founding movements in **1892**:

1.  **The Pennsylvania Chautauqua:** Founded by members of the Evangelical United Brethren, this movement modeled itself after the original Chautauqua Institution (1874, New York). They built a vaulted conical-roofed outdoor auditorium (the Playhouse) and a Hall of Philosophy for lectures, concerts, and religious services, subsequently constructing summer cottages [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].
2.  **The Camp Meeting:** The United Brethren also established a camp meeting across Pinch Road, hiring the same builder to construct a Tabernacle for religious services and Bible meetings. Worshipers built 100 cottages around tent plots [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

### Religious and Cultural History
The initial success of Mount Gretna was rooted in both educational and religious gatherings. The **Chautauqua** provided structured learning alongside leisure, while the **Camp Meeting** provided a dedicated space for Bible conferences and worship [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

**Cultural History:** The town experienced a cultural peak in the early 20th century, hosting concerts, lectures, and trade shows [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/]. Following a period of decline, a modern cultural revival began around **1976** with the **First Annual Outdoor Art Show**, initiated by local artists (Bruce Johnson, Reed Dixon, and John Wenzler). This fostered the growth of **Gretna Theatre** and **Music at Gretna**, establishing the community as a recognized regional center for arts and culture [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

### Military History
Military activity began relatively early in the town's development; the **Pennsylvania National Guard** started a 50-year annual encampment at Mt. Gretna in **1885** [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/]. Mount Gretna served as the state's first dedicated permanent training area. Furthermore, Mount Gretna is noted as a predecessor site to **Fort Indiantown Gap** [Source: https://www.ftig.ng.mil/About-Us/News/Article/4232222/mount-gretna-fort-indiantown-gaps-predecessor/].

### Summer Recreation Site Status and Attractions
Mount Gretna initially thrived as an early amusement park destination. Attractions included a stone fountain, an elaborate carousel, a primitive roller coaster called a “switch-back,” and a dancing pavilion [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

In **1885**, Conewago Creek was dammed to form **Lake Conewago**, which became a central feature for swimming and canoeing [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/]. The narrow gauge railroad (1889) allowed visitors to reach the top of Governor Dick Hill for expansive views [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

The peak recreational period lasted for about two decades. However, the rise of the **automobile** led to decline after the 1920s, compounded by the Depression and the departure of the National Guard in 1933. The amusement park closed, and the narrow gauge was abandoned [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

### Businesses Since Founding
Several businesses have existed in Mount Gretna since its founding, though many have closed and reopened:

*   **Early Businesses:** The initial attractions included park facilities, and lodging/retail included the **Chautauqua Inn**, **The Conewago Hotel** (1909, known for early modern amenities like private baths and telephones), **Kaufman’s Store and Hotel**, and **The Jigger Shop Ice cream parlor** [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].
*   **Enduring/Later Businesses:** The **Jigger Shop** continued to operate later in the century. The **Chautauqua Inn** survived the closures of other large hotels, though it was eventually demolished in **1970** due to modern fire codes and liability concerns [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/]. The **Timber Restaurant** was built in the **1960s** [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/]. Today, the arts and cultural organizations (Gretna Theatre, Music at Gretna) and local businesses supporting the Art Show provide economic support [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].

**Note on Continuity:** While many early establishments have closed (e.g., the Conewago Hotel, Kaufman Hotel), the *tradition* of gathering—in the Playhouse, at the Campmeeting, on the porches, and through the Jigger Shop—has been a constant thread throughout the town's history [Source: https://mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/].
